questions.question: How do you structure behavioral answers — STAR, but senior: what makes the difference in HR rounds?
questions.title: Star Answers
questions.direct_answer: STAR (Situation → Task → Action → Result) is the skeleton; the quality lives in the proportions: Situation/Task ≤ 20% (one or two sentences of context — not the story), Action 60% (WHAT YOU DID, decisions and trade-offs in first person — 'I chose X because', not 'we did'), Result 20% (outcomes with NUMBERS when possible + what you learned). The senior additions: a CONFLICT/COLLABORATION bank (disagreement handled well: 'my teammate wanted X, I advocated Y, we resolved by Z' — evidence-first, no villain), a FAILURE with a real root cause (not 'I worked too hard' — a misjudgment + the system you now use to prevent it), and QUESTIONS you ask THEM (the round's actual signal: curiosity about the team's real problems — 'what does the biggest tech-debt item cost you weekly?'). Prepare 6-8 stories covering the themes: hard technical decision, mistake, conflict, initiative, learning-fast, and leadership-without-title — each re-croppable for multiple question phrasings.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The structure with proportions:

```text
SITUATION + TASK   ≤ 20% — 1-2 sentences: the setting + what was
                              at stake. If the listener needs more
                              context than that, the story is the
                              wrong one (or needs cropping).
ACTION             ~60% — WHAT YOU DID, in first person:
                              the decision, the trade-off, the
                              specific steps. 'I pushed for X because
                              Y; I built Z; I convinced A by showing B.'
                              The 'I' is not ego — it's evidence of
                              YOUR contribution. 'We shipped it'
                              answers nothing about you.
RESULT             ~20% — outcomes + numbers when you have them
                              (latency, adoption, defects, time saved)
                              + the LEARNING (what you'd do differently
                              or now do by default).
```

The story bank (6-8 re-croppable stories): prepare one per theme — the hard technical decision (options → criteria → choice → aftermath); the mistake with a REAL root cause ('I assumed X; the fix was a checklist/system, not vigilance'); the disagreement resolved well (their view stated FAIRLY, your evidence, the resolution — no villains); the initiative beyond your role; learning something fast under pressure; leading without authority. Each story should re-crop: the 'mistake' story answers 'tell me about a conflict' when the mistake involved a disagreement, 'a time you failed' and 'a time you got feedback' when framed by outcome — prepare the NUCLEUS of each, not a script.

The questions you ask THEM (the strongest passive signal of the round): specific-to-them, not generic ('what does success look like' is filler). Good forms: 'What's the biggest engineering-debt item on this team, and what does it cost weekly?' / 'When the last person in this role struggled, what did that look like?' / 'How do decisions actually get made here — who breaks ties?' — curiosity about their REAL problems signals you're evaluating them too (the senior posture).

The honesty rules (the trust layer): never claim work you can't defend for 10 follow-up minutes; a real 'I don't know, here's how I'd find out' beats a bluff (interviewers probe until the bluff cracks — and they always probe); and frame past-employer problems without bitterness (what you LEARNED, not who was wrong).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q[behavioral question] --> BANK{story bank match}
    BANK --> S[situation + task — 2 sentences max]
    S --> A[action 60% — I decided, I built, I convinced — first person]
    A --> R[result 20% — numbers + learning]
    THEMES[6-8 stories: decision, mistake, conflict, initiative, learning, leadership]
    THEMES --> RECROP[each re-croppable across question phrasings]
    ASK[your questions for them] --> SIGNAL[specific curiosity — the senior posture]
    HONESTY[no undefended claims] --> PROBE[they WILL probe — 'how I'd find out' beats bluff]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why proportions matter (the interview's mechanics): interviewers calibrate on signal-per-minute — the situation you spent 3 minutes establishing is context THEY didn't ask for; the actions are the only part that discriminates candidates (everyone had situations; not everyone made the decisions). The 'we' pattern specifically erases the evidence: interviewers can't credit an invisible contribution — the fix is grammatical ('We built it; MY part was the data layer — I chose X because...') — team-crediting AND self-evidencing in one sentence.

The follow-up depth test (what actually separates prepared from performed): a real story survives 4-5 probe questions (why that approach, what were the alternatives, who disagreed, what broke after, what would you change now) because you lived the details; an invented or borrowed story collapses on the second. That's why the method is a BANK OF REAL NUCLEI: bullet the true facts (situation, decision points, the actual numbers you remember, the actual lesson), rehearse the CROPPING not the wording — a memorized script sounds memorized the moment a probe bends it, while real facts re-assemble fluidly under any phrasing.

The calibrated-truth nuance (the senior-level negotiation layer): numbers you don't remember exactly should be ranged honestly ('on the order of a 30-40% drop in p95') — ranged precision reads as memory, fake precision reads as construction. And the failure story's real differentiator isn't the failure, it's the SYSTEM-LEVEL fix ('I now write the test that would have caught this before touching the bug — that habit came from this story') — individual vigilance is a weak answer; a changed default behavior is a strong one. The last senior habit: end every behavioral round by asking which of your answers the interviewer found weakest — self-assessment in front of them, the same posture the job requires.
